extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and construing means- (or step-) plus-function claim limitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) / pre-AIA sixth paragraph, including definiteness, written description/enablement support, identification of corresponding structure, prior-art equivalence, and prosecution-record practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding structure/material/acts requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A means- (or step-) plus-function limitation must have corresponding structure, material, or acts disclosed in the specification that perform the recited function; where the specification discloses such corresponding structure the claim may be definite under 35 U.S.C. 112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one skilled in the art would recognize the structure for performing the function (e.g., a general/special purpose computer for performing complex computations), the disclosure may suffice. If not, applicant must amend the specification to include the relevant portions of any incorporated-by-reference material that correspond to the means- (or step-) plus-function limitation (37 CFR 1.57(c)(3)). Applicant should include only the relevant portions, not entire referenced documents. See In re Mott; Intel; Atmel; B. Braun; Medical Instrumentation & Diagnostic Corp. examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amend specification when corresponding structure not identifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: If one skilled in the art would not be able to identify the structure, material or acts from the specification to perform the recited function, the applicant will be required to amend the specification to contain the material incorporated by reference, including a clear link or associated structure, material or acts to the function recited in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require inserting entire referenced document; include only relevant portions corresponding to the means- (or step-) plus-function limitation. See 37 CFR 1.57(c)(3) and Atmel guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere restatement of function is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely restating a function associated with a means-plus-function limitation in the specification is insufficient to provide the corresponding structure for definiteness or for written description support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Noah; Blackboard; Aristocrat. A mere restatement without description of means that accomplish the function will likely fail 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description) as well as 112(b) (definiteness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function limitations must be analyzed for written description/enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: A means- (or step-) plus-function limitation that is indefinite for lack of disclosed corresponding structure may also lack adequate written description and/or enablement to support the full scope of the claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112, first paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional genus claims must show the applicant invented species sufficient to support the claimed functionally-defined genus; otherwise written description/enablement rejections may be appropriate. See Ariad (en banc) discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider all parts of the original disclosure for 112(a) support
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing whether 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112, first paragraph) support exists for a limitation, the examiner must consider the original disclosure in the summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, drawings, and other original application material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: In re Mott; In re Anderson; Hill-Rom v. Kinetic Concepts; In re Armbruster; Vas-Cath; In re Wolfensperger. Drawings and abstracts can supply support.

rubrics_metrics.name: If spec implicitly discloses corresponding structure, clarify record or require amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the written description only implicitly or inherently sets forth the corresponding structure/material/acts and the examiner concludes a POSITA would recognize it, the examiner should either (A) have the applicant amend the written description to expressly recite what structure/material/acts perform the function, or (B) state on the record what those structure/material/acts are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner may require amendment under 37 CFR 1.75(d) and MPEP § 608.01(o), provided no new matter is added. If the examiner identifies corresponding structure, they may state it in the Office action to clarify prosecution record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that cannot invoke 112(f) are not limited to disclosed structure
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim element cannot properly invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA sixth paragraph), it is not limited to the structure, material or act disclosed in the specification that performs the claimed function and will cover all means of performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single means claims that therefore cover every conceivable means for achieving the stated result risk non-enablement and can be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). See In re Hyatt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret multiple functional limitations as separate elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim recites multiple functions (common in computer-implemented inventions), each separately recited function should be interpreted as a separate element subject to treatment under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) if appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A generic placeholder (e.g., 'system configured to: extract...; compare...') does not avoid invoking 112(f); treat each function as a separate section 112(f) limitation as appropriate. Example demonstrates breaking 'system configured to' into two separate limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single means claim identification and risk
rubrics_metrics.description: A single means claim recites a means-plus-function limitation as the only limitation of a claim; 35 U.S.C. 112(f) applies only to 'an element in a claim for a combination' so single means claims may fail to be treated as a combination and risk non-enablement or overbreadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyatt held single means claims covering every conceivable means are nonenabling for the claimed scope. Examiner should identify when a claim is a 'single means' claim and consider 112(a) rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure prosecution record clearly states 112(f) interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examiner interprets a claim limitation under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the Office action should specify that the examiner has done so and explain reasons; if non-standard terms (other than 'means'/'step') are treated as invoking 112(f), the reasons should be clearly stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office action can state that a claim limitation is functional language coupled to a generic placeholder (e.g., 'module for') that does not connote structure and therefore invokes 112(f). If corresponding structure is determined, the Office action may specify it. Establish rebuttable presumptions on the record and explain any rebuttals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptions regarding use/absence of 'means' or 'step'
rubrics_metrics.description: Two rebuttable presumptions: (1) Using 'means' or 'step' creates a presumption the claim element is to be treated under 35 U.S.C. 112(f); (2) Absence of 'means' or 'step' creates a presumption the element is not to be treated under 112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first presumption is rebutted when 'means'/'step' is not modified by function or when the function is recited with sufficient structure/material within the claim. The second is rebutted when the claim element recites function but fails to recite sufficiently definite structure or material. See MPEP § 706.03 for form paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt to identify corresponding structure to facilitate prior art search
rubrics_metrics.description: If the corresponding structure for the claimed function is not clearly identifiable in the specification, the Office action should nevertheless attempt to identify the structure most closely associated with the means- (or step-) plus-function limitation to facilitate a prior art search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is especially important where multiple disclosed implementations might support the limitation and there may be confusion about which implementation is relied upon. See subsection II.B.

rubrics_metrics.name: When allowing a claim treated under 112(f), indicate it in reasons for allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: If allowing a claim that was treated under 35 U.S.C. 112(f), the examiner should indicate that the claim was interpreted under 112(f) or pre-AIA sixth paragraph in the reasons for allowance, and clarify the associated structure if not previously made of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides public notice of the claim construction used by the examiner during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art application to means-plus-function requires identical function and equivalence analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of a prior art reference to a means- (or step-) plus-function limitation requires that the prior art element perform the identical function specified in the claim, and the examiner bears the initial burden of showing the prior art structure or step is the same as or equivalent to the corresponding structure/material/acts described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior art teaches identity of function only, examiner must show a 'sound basis for believing' the prior art structure/acts could perform the claimed function (In re Spada). See MPEP § 2114 for inherency standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step claim construction for means-plus-function
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing a means-plus-function limitation involves two steps: (1) define the particular function of the claim limitation (the functional boundaries contained in the claim language), and (2) look to the specification/prosecution history for the corresponding structure that performs that function and is clearly linked or associated to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Budde; Cardiac Pacemakers; Golight; B. Braun; Elekta. The corresponding structure must be clearly linked/associated in spec or prosecution history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie case of equivalence – examiner burden and required explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner finds (A) the prior art element performs the claimed function, (B) is not excluded by any explicit definition in the specification for an equivalent, and (C) is an equivalent of the means- (or step-) plus-function limitation, the examiner should provide an explanation and rationale in the Office action for why the prior art element is an equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prima facie case of equivalence is made, the examiner should explain why and identify supporting factors/case law (e.g., In re Bond).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors supporting a conclusion of equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that support concluding the prior art element is an equivalent include: (A) the prior art element performs the identical function in substantially the same way and produces substantially the same results; (B) a person of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the interchangeability of the prior art element for the corresponding element disclosed in the specification; (C) there are insubstantial differences between the prior art element and the corresponding element disclosed in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Kemco Sales; Odetics; Deere & Co.; Al-Site; Chiuminatta; IMS Technology; Warner-Jenkinson; Caterpillar cases. Examiner should show at least one factor to support equivalence and then may also explain why substitution would have been obvious (In re Brown).

rubrics_metrics.name: If nonequivalence not shown, examiner must still consider obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where applicant shows that a prior art element is not equivalent to the structure/material/acts described in the specification, the examiner must still perform a 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness) analysis to determine if the claimed means- (or step-) plus-function is obvious from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding of nonequivalence prevents anticipation but does not prevent an obviousness rejection. Examiner may apply 102/103 rejections where appropriate, and may rely on alternative grounds when prior art elements differ but together render the claim obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on applicant to show nonequivalence and acceptable evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the examiner makes out a prima facie case of equivalence, the burden shifts to the applicant to show that the prior art element is not an equivalent of the structure/material/acts disclosed in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant's evidence may include: (A) teachings in the applicant's specification that particular prior art is not equivalent; (B) teachings in the prior art reference itself showing nonequivalence; (C) 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit evidence demonstrating facts tending to show nonequivalence. Examiner must ensure applicant's interpretation is consistent with the specification and weigh indicia presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification can narrow or broaden scope of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a means-plus-function limitation is limited to particular structures/materials/acts or covers any and all structures performing the claimed function depends on how the specification treats equivalents: the spec may limit the claim to disclosed embodiments or allow coverage of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only one embodiment is described, corresponding structure may be limited to that embodiment and equivalents (NOMOS); conversely, allowing equivalents too broadly can render the claim so broad as to encompass any means for performing the function (In re Meyer; In re Abele; In re Walter). Examiner must interpret scope case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere allegations of nonequivalence are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should not accept as persuasive a bare statement or opinion that a prior art element is not an equivalent. Applicant must present substantive indicia or evidence supporting nonequivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant argues that means- (or step-) plus-function language is limited to certain specific characteristics not described in the specification, the claim should not be allowed until amended to recite those specific structural or additional functional characteristics; otherwise the claim could be allowed with broad functional language contrary to public notice policy.
